{{short description|Several types of mathematical matrix containing zeroes}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''hollow matrix''' may refer to one of several related classes of [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]]: a sparse matrix; a matrix with a large block of zeroes; or a matrix with diagonal entries all zero.

==Definitions==

===Sparse===
A ''hollow matrix'' may be one with "few" non-zero entries: that is, a [[sparse matrix]].<ref>{{cite book | author=Pierre Massé | title=Optimal Investment Decisions: Rules for Action and Criteria for Choice | publisher=[[Prentice-Hall]] | year=1962 | page=142 }}</ref>

===Block of zeroes===
A ''hollow matrix'' may be a square {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix with an {{math|''r'' × ''s''}} block of zeroes where  {{math|''r'' + ''s'' > ''n''}}.<ref>{{cite book | author=Paul Cohn | authorlink=Paul Cohn | title=Free Ideal Rings and Localization in General Rings | url=https://archive.org/details/freeidealringslo00cohn | url-access=limited | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=2006 | isbn=0-521-85337-0 | page=[https://archive.org/details/freeidealringslo00cohn/page/n453 430] }}</ref>

===Diagonal entries all zero===
A ''hollow matrix'' may be a [[square matrix]] whose [[Diagonal#Matrices|diagonal]] elements are all equal to zero.<ref>{{cite book | author=James E. Gentle | title=Matrix Algebra: Theory, Computations, and Applications in Statistics | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=2007 | isbn=978-0-387-70872-0 | page=42 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PDjIV0iWa2cC&q=%22hollow+matrix%22}}</ref> That is, an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix {{math|1=''A'' = (''a<sub>ij</sub>'')}} is hollow if {{math|1=''a<sub>ij</sub>'' = 0}} whenever {{math|1=''i'' = ''j''}} (i.e. {{math|1=''a<sub>ii</sub>'' = 0}} for all {{mvar|i}}). The most obvious example is the [[real numbers|real]] [[skew-symmetric matrix|skew-symmetric]] matrix.  Other examples are the [[adjacency matrix]] of a finite [[simple graph]], and a [[distance matrix]] or [[Euclidean distance matrix]].

In other words, any square matrix that takes the form
<math display=block>\begin{pmatrix}
 0   & \ast & & \ast & \ast \\
\ast & 0    & & \ast & \ast \\
     & & \ddots \\
\ast & \ast & & 0 & \ast \\
\ast & \ast & & \ast & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>
is a hollow matrix, where the symbol <math>\ast</math> denotes an arbitrary entry.

For example,
<math display=block>\begin{pmatrix}
 0 & 2 &  6 & \frac{1}{3} & 4 \\
 2 & 0 &  4 & 8 & 0 \\
 9 & 4 &  0 & 2 & 933 \\
 1 & 4 &  4 & 0 & 6 \\
 7 & 9 & 23 & 8 & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>
is a hollow matrix.

==Properties==

*The [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of a hollow matrix is zero.
*If {{mvar|L}} represents a [[linear map]] <math>L:V \to V</math>with respect to a fixed [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]], then it maps each basis vector {{math|'''e'''}} into the [[Complement (set theory)|complement]] of the [[Linear span|span]] of {{math|'''e'''}}. That is, <math>L(\langle e \rangle) \cap \langle e \rangle = \langle 0 \rangle</math> where <math>\langle e \rangle = \{ \lambda e : \lambda \in F\}.</math>
*The [[Gershgorin circle theorem]] shows that the moduli of the [[eigenvalue]]s of a hollow matrix are less or equal to the sum of the moduli of the non-diagonal row entries.
